extracted.intended_audience: authors, freelance editors, publishing professionals, and students interested in editing/publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the role, scope, timing, and tasks of developmental editors across fiction, nonfiction, textbooks, and academic manuscripts, including ethical boundaries and typical deliverables. Useful for authors, editors, and publishers deciding when and how to use developmental editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of developmental editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Developmental editing is a form of writing support that comes into play before or during the production of a publishable manuscript... involves 'significant structuring or restructuring of a manuscript's discourse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames developmental editing as large-scale work on organization and discourse rather than minor copy edits; it applies across fiction, non-fiction, and academic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Developmental editing comes into play before or during the production of a publishable manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may be engaged early to help conceive and plan a project or later when a draft requires substantial revision; the timing affects the nature of the editor's work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding conception, structure, and outline
rubrics_metrics.description: A developmental editor may guide an author (or group of authors) in conceiving the topic, planning the overall structure, and developing an outline—and may coach authors in their writing, chapter by chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This represents the 'true' or full-range developmental edit where the editor helps form the project rather than only polishing text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete developmental edit (organization and restructuring)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete developmental edit involves addressing organization and restructuring the manuscript, such as moving content from one chapter to another and requesting additional content from the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical actions include reorganizing chapters, identifying missing material, and advising on where to add or remove content; editors typically recommend rather than directly change content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common engagement after publisher-initiated revision
rubrics_metrics.description: More commonly, a developmental editor is engaged only after someone (usually the publisher) decides that the authors' draft requires substantial revision and restructuring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In these cases developmental editing functions as a radical form of substantive editing—focused on major revision rather than early project conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author control and limits of editorial changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrespective of when the developmental editor is brought into a writing project, authors retain control over the document and are responsible for providing the content. Developmental editors typically don't make the changes directly to the manuscript but instead provide guidance and suggestions, although some 'hands-on editing is used to illustrate principles of craft and mechanics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain authorial control; use hands-on edits sparingly to demonstrate techniques. If an editor creates significant amounts of content, they may be considered a contributing author or ghostwriter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding ghostwriting / ethical boundary
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor who creates significant amounts of content is no longer an editor but a contributing author or a ghostwriter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly in academic contexts, editors must ensure they do not engage in ghost writing if authorship is not intended; editors' duties should remain editorial, not authorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliverable — editorial letter of main suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: After completing a developmental edit, an editor typically provides a letter to the author (often in the form of an email) explaining the main suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The letter summarizes the large-scale recommendations and next steps rather than presenting a fully rewritten manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role in textbook publishing (project management and content control)
rubrics_metrics.description: In textbook publishing, developmental editors are involved from the beginning, and often serve as the book's project manager... may be responsible for creating the outline to guide the author's writing—and may also prepare short parts of text, such as legends, exercises, and supporting materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because publishers often decide content, scope, and level, developmental editors for textbooks may manage length, edit the developing manuscript, and instruct artists—a more hands-on and managerial role than for trade books.

rubrics_metrics.name: When developmental editing is useful in academic research
rubrics_metrics.description: Developmental editing in research is useful in two main situations: researchers who struggle to produce a manuscript likely to pass peer review may seek assistance during writing, and those facing repeated journal rejections may require help addressing complex reviewer comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support often extends beyond editing into mentoring; professional and ethical considerations apply—editors should provide editorial (not authorial) assistance and be mindful of authorship and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental editing as mentoring and part of support services
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors' editors, academic writing instructors, and translators may provide developmental editing alongside other support services, such as writing education, translation, and linguistic editing... Developmental editing-based mentoring programs have been implemented by journals and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This highlights developmental editing's educational component: teaching craft and publishing norms as part of improving manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction editing tasks split: structure, narrative, and language
rubrics_metrics.description: Adam O'Connor Rodriguez splits the tasks of developmental fiction editing into three main parts: structure, narrative, and language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure = length, order, pacing; Narrative = characters, major scenes, pacing, big-picture elements; Language = dialogue, physical description, sensory information, sentence structure. Use this tripartite lens to diagnose and prescribe changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific fiction interventions (plot, characters, scenes)
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor would provide ideas for fixing plot holes, inconsistencies in characters, scenes that need more depth, and scenes that need to be cut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical, actionable suggestions target plot coherence, character consistency, scene-level depth, and economy; editors may flag and recommend cuts as well as expansions.
